section_structure.heading: [Introduction — untitled opening]
section_structure.summary: Caston frames the puzzle: De anima 3.3 introduces phantasia as a distinct, new capacity, but its motivation is left unclear. The treatise has only mentioned phantasia in passing and the chapter's 'serpentine argument' nowhere announces its motives in a forthright way. Caston announces a methodological commitment: rather than illuminate the chapter via the British Empiricists, Kant, or Wittgenstein (the standard secondary-literature move), one must start by asking why Aristotle needs phantasia in the first place. His thesis: a close reading of the chapter's opening reveals that DA 3.3 is centrally concerned with the problem of error — the problem of explaining how the content of mental states could ever diverge from what is actually in the world. Aristotle poses this as a difficulty for his predecessors' views on perception and thought, but the same complaint applies to his own theory of sensation and conception (αἴσθησις, νόησις/φρόνησις), which he regards as the most basic forms of perception and thought. Caston suggests: this is why Aristotle introduces phantasia — to preempt charges that he cannot explain the possibility of error himself. For the strategy to work he must show (a) phantasia is distinct from sensation and conception, and (b) its content can admit of error. That is the project of the remainder of DA 3.3.

section_structure.heading: I. The Position of De anima 3.3
section_structure.summary: Architectural justification for phantasia's placement. DA's first half is foundational (predecessors at 1.1-1.5 + definition of soul at 2.1-2.3); it then ascends through the basic powers along the hierarchy of living kinds — plant powers (2.4 nutrition/growth/reproduction), perception (2.5-3.2), and conceptual/reasoning powers exclusive to humans (3.4-3.8). The chapter sequence mirrors Aristotle's hierarchy in soul and in nature. Other powers (desire, action: 3.9-3.11) are deferred since they are nearly coextensive with the perceptual powers. Phantasia breaks this pattern: it belongs to every (or almost every) animal but is treated separately at the critical juncture between perception and thought (DA 3.3). Caston entertains the editorial-accident hypothesis (citing Lewes 1864 in fn. 10 with sardonic relish) but rejects it: phantasia is somehow necessary at this stage, prior to Aristotle's accounts of thought, desire, and action. The opening sentence of 3.3 (427a17-20) restates the leitmotif criteria of motion and perception, expanded to include thinking. The first third of 3.3 is a concerted attack on the thesis that thought is crucially LIKE perception — an attack that requires a distinct new ability, like phantasia. The argument turns on the problem of error.

section_structure.heading: II. The Thesis that Thinking and Perceiving are 'the Same'
section_structure.summary: Aristotle opens DA 3.3 by setting up the thesis that thinking is like perceiving as a respected predecessor view (ἔνδοξον). Two reasons supposedly support it: (i) both are cognitive attitudes — 'the soul discriminates and knows something that is' (427a20-21); (ii) more weightily, the ancients say 'thinking and perceiving are the same' (427a21-22), backed by citations from Empedocles (DK 31 B 106, B 108), Parmenides, Anaxagoras, and Homer (Od. 18.136). Caston notes the evidence is frail: none of the citations mentions perception, and the second in original context is not even about thinking. They share only the general position that thought depends in some way on environment/bodily condition. Caston follows Rodier, Hicks, Apelt, and Ross in punctuating so that only one such reason is offered. Aristotle's appeal to inference is a silent admission he can defend only the modest claim that his predecessors are COMMITTED to thinking-perceiving identity, whether or not they say it explicitly. Caston distinguishes two readings: (1) thinking is the same KIND of process as perceiving, and (1') thinking does not differ from perceiving in any way at all. Theophrastus' formula τὸ αὐτὸν ἢ παραπλήσιον ('the same or nearly the same,' De sens. 10, 502.7-9 Diels Doxogr.) supports the weaker reading (1). Aristotle then offers two further reasons on his predecessors' behalf: (2) thinking and perceiving are both bodily processes; (3) one thinks and perceives like by like. Neither is necessary, but each is sufficient for (1).

section_structure.heading: III. The Problem of Error
section_structure.summary: The heart of the article. Aristotle now turns to ATTACK the thesis that thinking and perceiving are the same. He directs attention to the widespread phenomenon of error and challenges his predecessors to account for it: 'they should have said something about being in error, since this is particularly endemic to animals and the soul spends a lot of time in this state' (DA 3.3, 427a29-b2). Caston stresses Aristotle's etymological force in οἰκειότερον ('more endemic') and πλείω ('more') — animals spend MORE time in error than in veridical cognition; this conflicts with Aristotle's general epistemological outlook (perceptual apparatus discriminates real differences in the environment, De sens. 1, 436b18-437a3; cf. De an. 3.12, 434a30-b1), so it is a polemical exaggeration in the service of the dilemma. Aristotle taunts his predecessors with a dilemma: given their views, it is necessary either (i) all appearances are true, or (ii) error is contact with what is unlike (since that is the opposite of recognizing like by like) (427b2-5). Neither horn is acceptable; each is a REDUCTIO AD ABSURDUM. Caston traces the affinity to a Platonic argument in Theaetetus 151E-157D (esp. 152C; the Secret Doctrine at 152D): Socrates argues thesis A (knowledge is perception) is linked to thesis B (all appearances are true) and the Heraclitean Secret Doctrine C. But the differences are sharp: Aristotle's interests are psychological, not epistemological. The argument is reformulated: (3) one thinks/perceives like by like, broken into (3a) one perceives/thinks whenever like is affected by like, and (3b) whatever one perceives or thinks on a given occasion corresponds exactly to whatever brings that state about. (3a) and (3b) are logically independent. (3) implies (4) whatever one perceives or thinks on a given occasion corresponds exactly to something in the environment — and thus (5) all appearances are true, if extended to ALL token mental states. (5) follows just as the first horn of the dilemma states. To allow for error, an adherent of (3) must RESTRICT its scope to veridical states — but then (3) cannot explain the content of nonveridical states, falling back on the second horn (error as unlike-by-unlike). The dilemma is genuine.

section_structure.heading: III.B The Second Horn of the Dilemma
section_structure.summary: Aristotle cannot rule the second horn out as absurd. He acknowledges error exists. The compressed objection: 'both error and knowledge of contraries seem to be the same' (427b5-6). This is not Aristotle's own view but what he takes to follow from the second horn. Reconstruction: if error were the interaction of unlikes, then in the case of contraries (one knows pairs of contraries simultaneously, on the rule that 'a contrary state is recognized from its contrary,' EN 5.1 1129a17ff., cf. DA 3.6 430b21-24, DA 1.5 411a3-7), error and knowledge would coincide — absurd. So error cannot be due to interaction of unlikes. Aristotle's reductio reasonably refutes the second horn even though it relies on a tacit premise (the contraries-rule). Caston notes Aristotle's free use of contestable premises — they are independently reputable; this is not ad hominem but a reasonable judge's verdict. The further significance: Aristotle himself, faced with the dilemma, could not accept the second horn (error-as-unlike-by-unlike); he is therefore driven toward the first horn, which he considers anathema.

section_structure.heading: IV. The Thesis that All Appearances are True
section_structure.summary: Caston now interrogates whether (5) genuinely follows. The strict route requires (3) on all-token reading. But Aristotle's predecessors hold (1) and various supports; the route via (2) (bodily processes) is too weak (the Phaedo author would not infer infallibility from corporeality). The route via (3) is the one that yields the dilemma. Aristotle himself, in Metaphysics 4.5, 1009b12-17, gives a different route: 'because they suppose perception is thought and this is alteration, perceptual appearance is of necessity true' — appealing to (6) thinking and perceiving are both alterations (ἀλλοιώσεις). This widens the scope: it captures Anaxagoras (who rejects bodily process (2)) and Theophrastus-on-Empedocles/Democritus types (who emphasize alteration in the body determining the content of mental states). Caston exegetes Metaphysics 4.5, 1009b17-31 at length: Aristotle's predecessors take thinking as 'in a different state' — and so all mental contents are determined by bodily alteration. The Empedocles/Parmenides/Homer citations stress: thinking changes with bodily condition. The Anaxagoras case is special — for Anaxagoras, intellect is 'simple, unmixed, and pure' (DA 1.2, 405a16-17; 3.4, 429a18) and 'has nothing in common with anything' (DA 1.2, 405b21; 3.4, 429b24); Anaxagoras cannot endorse (3a) but can accept (3b) — content determined by what brings the state about. Caston notes Anaxagoras is the canonical exception, but (3b) suffices to commit him to (5). The general formulation: where content is exhaustively determined by cause, error is impossible.

section_structure.heading: V. Aristotle's Dilemma
section_structure.summary: Caston's pivotal move: Aristotle's critique of his predecessors REBOUNDS ON HIMSELF. Aristotle is committed to a version of (1): 'the intellect is related to the objects of conception in just the same way as the sense can sense to the objects of sense' (DA 3.4, 429a16-17). The various disanalogies (the intellect is not the activity of a bodily organ, DA 3.4 429a18-27; De gen. anim. 2.3, 736b28-29) do not free him from the problem. Aristotle also endorses a version of (3) at DA 2.5: theorists like Anaxagoras are right only to the extent that the sense must INITIALLY be unlike the object in actuality, but must be POTENTIALLY like and during sensation BECOMES like (417a17-20, 418a3-6; 3.2, 425b22-23). The likeness occurring during sensation shows Aristotle is fully committed to the cause-content correspondence: sensation, for Aristotle, is clearly about its cause. The account of conceiving in DA 3.4 is framed in similar terms (429a13-18); at the outset, the conceptual capacity is like its objects only in potentiality; during conception it becomes like its object in actuality, as a result of the object's acting on it (430a3-5; cf. 3.8, 431b28-29; Metaph. 12.7, 1072a30). In both sensation and conception, content and cause COINCIDE. Aristotle accepts a version of (3a). So long as these states are about what brings them about, the relevant 'appearances' will always be true. The same holds for (6): Aristotle's hesitation about describing sensation/conception as 'alterations' is entirely due to his technical usage; in the broader sense at issue in (6), he remains vulnerable. To use Aristotle's own metaphor: sensation and conception are like 'making contact' (θιγγάνειν, Metaph. 9.10, 1051b24-25) — they either work or not at all. At DA 2.5, 417b24-26 the object of sensation must exist. There is a sense in which all appearances are TRUE FOR ARISTOTLE: namely, all those appearances that arise from sensation and conception, the most basic operations. This is the key restriction. (3b) holds for him only for these types — but he can EVADE the disastrous consequences of the first horn because not all kinds of mental states operate under this model. Imagination, memory, expectation, thought, reasoning, desire, deliberation, action, passions, dreams all require phantasia (and Aristotle identifies the 'change brought about by the functioning of sensation' as phantasia, 428b25-26, 429a1; De insomn. 1, 459a17-18). Phantasia is the key — it can be at variance with reality. Likewise, thought (combination of concepts, predication, inference) goes beyond simple conception (only the conception of simple incomposites and indivisibles is infallible: DA 3.6, 430a26-27, b27-28; Metaph. 9.10, 1051b15-32, 1052a1-4). Higher functions, error, content explanation in general — all rest on phantasia. The chapter then must show that phantasia is not subject to the same difficulties. Caston: 'It does not matter whether phantasia is, like Molière's virtus dormativa, just a problem redescribed as a solution. Aristotle must offer a positive account.'

section_structure.heading: VI. Distinguishing Capacities
section_structure.summary: Caston tracks Aristotle's strategy: phantasia must be (1) not identical with sensation or conception, and (2) its content must be explained differently. In the long middle section (427b6-428b9), Aristotle argues phantasia differs from (a) sensation (428a5-18); (b) conceptions (428a17); (c) knowledge (428a18); (d) belief (427b16-24, 428a18-24); (e) a complex of belief and sensation (428a24-b9, Plato's Sophist 264AB / Timaeus 52A target). Caston identifies two kinds of nonidentity arguments in Aristotle: (i) two powers may be EXTENSIONALLY differentiated (not coinstantiated), and (ii) the powers may differ 'in being' (τῷ εἶναι), even if always coinstantiated (De insomn. 1, 459a16-18). Extensional arguments: not all animals think (427b7-8, b12-14), so sensation ≠ thinking; phantasia exists where reason does not (428a24; cf. 427b8, b13-14), so phantasia ≠ belief. Phantasia vs. sensation extension is less clear: 'there seem to be' animals with sensation but not phantasia (δοκεῖ, 428b8-11), but evidence outside the chapter commits Aristotle to strict coextension. The decisive nonidentity argument: phantasia can be FALSE (428a11-12, b17-18); sensation, conception, knowledge are always true (427b12, 428a11-12, 428a17-18); belief can be false too (428a12, b17); but belief differs in extension and conviction (πίστις, 428a19-24). So phantasia, sensation, belief — all distinct. Phantasia stands MIDWAY between intellectual and perceptual powers: more basic, extends to all animal kingdom, capable of error, doesn't require conviction, bears content in a neutral way. Belief admits/rejects, is affected emotionally; phantasia can remain emotionally unaffected by its contents (3.3, 427a23-24). Phantasia thus suits Aristotle's explanatory needs for accounting for animal error.

section_structure.heading: VII. Phantasia and Error
section_structure.summary: Aristotle now provides the positive aetiology: how phantasia can be false (DA 3.3, 428b10-429a9). Causal factors continue to explain content, but DIFFERENTLY than for sensation: this is what permits falsehood and the consequent plasticity of animal behavior. The aetiology: in sensation, an object produces an initial stimulation (αἴσθημα) in the peripheral sense organs; this change travels to the central sense organ and produces the sensory experience (αἴσθησις). But a change can give rise to further changes; this initial stimulation can have INDIRECT effects. The 'change brought about by the functioning of sensation' (κίνησιν ὑπὸ τῆς ἐνεργείας τῆς αἰσθήσεως, 428b13) is necessarily similar to the sensation (ταύτην ὁμοίαν ἀνάγκη εἶναι τῇ αἰσθήσει, 428b14) — and from this it follows the second change can be false as well as true, making varied animal behavior possible (428b14-17). Later Aristotle explicitly identifies this 'change brought about by the functioning of sensation' as phantasia (428b25-26, 429a1; De insomn. 1, 459a17-18); residual effects similar to sensations remain (τὸ ἐμμένειν καὶ ὁμοίας εἶναι ταῖς αἰσθήσεσι, 429a4-5). Phantasia derives from sensation in two senses: (i) CAUSALLY derives from a particular sensation, and (ii) its CHARACTER derives from the character of that sensation. Phantasia is described elsewhere as 'a weak sort of sensation' (αἴσθησίς τις ἀσθενής, Rhet. 1.11, 1370a28). The echo analogy (Diagram 1, p. 47): when one shouts in a canyon, the initial air-disturbance produces an echo via the canyon wall. Phantasma is the echo, related indirectly to the original object through the αἴσθημα (Diagram 2, p. 48). Crucially: the phantasma is only an INDIRECT effect of the object of perception; the phantasma's content is not its causal antecedents but its CAUSAL POWERS, sometimes modified on the way to the central organ — by alcohol, sickness, dreaming (De insomn. 3, 461a8-24; Probl. 30.14, 957a5-15, a25-35). Caston's salamander/dragon example (p. 49): a phantasma originating from observing a salamander may, after alcohol, generate the dream of a dragon. A dragon need never have been perceived nor even exist. WHAT the phantasma is about is determined by its causal POWERS — its capacity to affect the central organ — not by its actual causal ancestors. Formal account (P): 'For any phantasma φ and time t, the total effect φ can produce at t on the central sense organ is the same as the total effect some sensory stimulation s could produce on the central sense organ, were s to occur; and at t, φ is about what ever s would be about.' This is confirmed at De insomn. 2, 460b18-27 and Metaph. 5.29, 1024b23-24 (scene-painting and dream are 'something but not what they produce a phantasia of' — and so are called false). Phantasia is QUASI-PERCEPTUAL: similar in TYPE of information it conveys. Phantasmata are not themselves viewed; they are powers, not tiny pictures. Falsehood in phantasia is not the propositional falsehood of language/discursive thought (Metaph. 9.10, 1051b1-6); it is a non-propositional misalignment between cause and content. This is significant for Aristotle's account of intentionality: a form of content/intentionality more basic than the conceptual, that does NOT require concepts or predication, can account for the mental lives of animals AND for much that occurs in humans (DA 3.3, 428b16-17, 429a5-6, 3.7-3.8).

section_structure.heading: VIII. Phantasia and Reliability
section_structure.summary: Specific conditions for true/false phantasia (428b17-30). Reliability depends on which type of perception is involved: proper perceptibles (colors, flavors), common perceptibles (shapes, motion), or incidental perceptibles (the so-called 'incidental percepts'). The latter two are already error-prone. But for proper perceptibles, Aristotle adds the qualification 'or it has falsehood to the least possible extent' (ἢ ὅτι ὀλίγιστον ἔχουσα τὸ ψεῦδος, 428b19). Caston: this qualification is inexplicable on Aristotle's account UNLESS phantasia is implicated. The worst case occurs when objects are very distant (428b29-30) — perception of size and magnitude is most error-prone (428b24-25). Aristotle's correlations among proper-vs-common-vs-incidental perception, concurrence-with-sensation, and reliability lead to surprising consequences: (i) a phantasia originating from a false sensation of a proper object will be TRUE so long as concurrent; (ii) a phantasia originating from a true sensation of a common/incidental object will be FALSE even if concurrent. Caston flags the puzzling result and concludes the section: these remarks depend on contingent assumptions about real-world functioning; they are not part of the central aetiology of error but a discussion of specific conditions.

section_structure.heading: IX. Conclusion
section_structure.summary: Summative statement. The opening of DA 3.3 tells us what the chapter is about: predecessors cannot account for error because they rely on overly simplistic content theories binding content too closely to cause. Aristotle's own account of sensation and conception is prey to the same problem. Though he does not advertise candidly, he sets about doing what needs to be done: there is nothing wrong with SOME mental capacities being infallible, even foundational ones like sensation and conception, so long as the content of OTHER mental states is not accounted for in the same way. Aristotle introduces a new capacity — phantasia — which depends on sensation (causally and in content) but successfully evades the dilemma via a more complicated aetiology appealing to CAUSAL POWERS rather than CAUSAL ANCESTORS. Phantasia provides the basis for the content of most intentional states without appealing to concepts or predication. Caston's polemical final paragraph: phantasia is NOT a 'locus of non-paradigmatic sensory experience' (Schofield 1978's phrase explicitly cited at fn. 70). The point is precisely that error is NORMAL in animal life and psychology must account for it. Caston signals the project of his forthcoming works (intentionality in Aristotle and in ancient Greek philosophy generally) and signs off 'Brown University.'

outline: Cluster 1 (PDF 1-2, book 20-21, untitled opening): Caston frames the puzzle. DA 3.3 introduces phantasia as a 'distinct, new capacity' but the chapter's 'serpentine argument' does not announce its motives forthrightly. The standard secondary-literature move — illuminate via British Empiricists, Kant, or Wittgenstein — gets things backwards. Aristotle stands at the beginning of this history when phantasia was not an established topic. To understand what he had in mind, one must start by asking why phantasia is introduced at all. A close reading of the chapter's opening — a passage scantly attended to in the literature (fn. 4) — reveals DA 3.3 is centrally concerned with THE PROBLEM OF ERROR: the problem of explaining how the content of mental states can ever diverge from what is actually in the world. Aristotle poses this as a difficulty for his predecessors but the same complaint applies to his own theory of sensation and conception (which he regards as the most basic forms of perception and thought).

Cluster 2 (PDF 2-3, book 22, opening cont.): Caston's master thesis: Aristotle introduces phantasia 'to preempt charges that he cannot explain the possibility of error himself.' For this strategy to work, two things must be shown: (a) phantasia is distinct from sensation and conception; (b) unlike them, its content genuinely DOES admit of error. That is what DA 3.3's remaining sections set out to do. Phantasia is also CRUCIAL for Aristotle's account of intentionality — his account of how mental states can be of or about things, or more generally possess content. Sensation and conception are intentional, but they cannot provide him with a general model for intentionality, since the content of most intentional states can fail to correspond to what is in the world. Phantasia can explain this possibility of error and Aristotle regularly appeals to it in explaining the content of other intentional states. DA 3.3 testifies to Aristotle's concern with problems arising from intentionality and his effort to solve them.

Cluster 3 (PDF 3-4, book 22-23, §I): The architectural placement of DA 3.3. The first half of DA is foundational (predecessors 1.1-1.5, definition of soul 2.1-2.3); the second ascends through the basic soul-powers in the hierarchy of living kinds — plant (2.4), perception (2.5-3.2), conceptual/reasoning (3.4-3.8). Other powers (desire, action: 3.9-3.11) are deferred since they are nearly coextensive with the perceptual powers. Phantasia BREAKS this pattern: it belongs to every (or almost every) animal but is treated separately at the critical juncture between perception and thought (DA 3.3). Caston rehearses Lewes's (1864) sardonic editorial-accident hypothesis (fn. 10) but rejects it as untenable in the face of generally coherent compositions. Phantasia is somehow necessary at this stage of exposition, prior to Aristotle's accounts of thought, desire, and action.

Cluster 4 (PDF 4, book 24, §I cont.): The opening sentence of DA 3.3 (427a17-20) recalls criteria for soul: (i) change in place; (ii) conceiving (νοεῖν, in a broad sense covering practical wisdom too), thinking, and perceiving. The criteria of motion and perception are a leitmotif in DA (1.2, 403a25-26; 1.2, 404b7-10, b28-30, 405b11-12; 1.5, 409b19-25; 3.9, 432a15-17 endorsement). The reformulation expands the perceptual criterion to include thinking; the second criterion 'thought is a kind of perceiving' is reputable but cannot stand as it is. The first third of DA 3.3 is a concerted attack on this view — one requiring phantasia to evade the consequences. The argument turns on the problem of error.

Cluster 5 (PDF 5-6, book 24-26, §II): The endoxon thesis that thinking is like perceiving. Two supports: (i) general similarity — both are cognitive attitudes ('the soul discriminates and knows something that is,' 427a20-21); (ii) more weightily, the ancients' formula τὸ φρονεῖν καὶ τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι ταὐτὸν εἶναι φασιν ('thinking and perceiving are the same,' 427a21-22), supported by citations from Empedocles (DK 31 B 106, B 108), Parmenides, Anaxagoras, Homer (Od. 18.136). The evidence is frail: none of the citations mentions perception; the second is not even about thinking in original context. Caston follows Rodier/Hicks/Apelt/Ross punctuation isolating one γάρ-reason. Aristotle's appeal is a silent admission he can defend only the modest claim that his predecessors are COMMITTED to this thesis, whether they say it or not.

Cluster 6 (PDF 6, book 26, §II cont.): Caston distinguishes (1) thinking consists in the SAME KIND of process as perceiving, and (1') thinking does not differ from perceiving in any way at all. Theophrastus' formula ἢ ταὐτὸν ἢ παραπαλήσιον ('the same or nearly the same,' De sens. 10, 502.7-9 Diels Doxogr.) supports (1). Aristotle offers two reasons on his predecessors' behalf: (2) thinking and perceiving are both bodily processes; (3) one thinks and perceives like by like. Each is sufficient for (1), neither necessary. Burnyeat's Theaetetus (1990) cited (fn. 22) as the classic account of the Platonic Secret Doctrine.

Cluster 7 (PDF 7, book 27, §III): Aristotle attacks. He directs attention to error as endemic and challenges his predecessors: 'they should have said something about being in error, too, since this is particularly endemic to animals and the soul spends a lot of time in this state' (DA 3.3, 427a29-b2). Caston stresses the comparatives οἰκειότερον and πλείω: animals spend MORE time in error than in veridical cognition — a claim that polemically exaggerates against Aristotle's general epistemological commitment (perceptual apparatus naturally discriminates real differences: De sens. 1, 436b18-437a3, cf. DA 3.12, 434a30-b1). The dilemma: either (i) all appearances are true, or (ii) contact with what is unlike is error (since like-by-like is recognition). Both are reductios — neither is acceptable.

Cluster 8 (PDF 7-8, book 27-28, §III cont.): The Platonic parallel. Theaetetus 151E-157D (Burnyeat 1990 cited fn. 22 again at 202.23-24): Socrates examines thesis A (knowledge = perception), thesis B (all appearances are true), and the 'Secret Doctrine' C (perception and what is perceived exist only in the interaction between subject and object). Plato names Empedocles and Homer among others (153E). The connections (Burnyeat: they mutually imply each other) suggest Aristotle drew inspiration from Plato. But: Aristotle's INTERESTS are different (psychological, not epistemological); the STRUCTURE of the arguments is different. Instead of the Secret Doctrine, Aristotle appeals to (2) and (3); his conclusion is NOT that all appearances are true (only one horn of his dilemma).

Cluster 9 (PDF 8, book 28, §III A 'First Horn'): Aristotle dismisses the first horn (all appearances are true) without argument — he is content to stand on its absurdity. Not always so complacent (cf. Metaph. 4.5; the same antirealism is anathema there). But here, psychology is not the place for such epistemological arguments. Error is a DATUM that must be accounted for if a theory is to count as a psychological theory at all. Aristotle's own theory must be measured against this desideratum too.

Cluster 10 (PDF 8-9, book 29-30, §III A cont.): The deep diagnosis. (1), the same-kind-of-process thesis, by itself hardly implies infallibility. (2), the bodily-process thesis, is not enough either — the Phaedo author would reject inferring infallibility from corporeality. It is (3), like-by-like, that leads to the dilemma. For when the Presocratic citations are taken in context, 'perceiving' and 'thinking' do not stand for two isolated processes, but rather ALL MENTAL STATES; and understood as a general thesis, (3) leaves very few alternatives.

Cluster 11 (PDF 9, book 29, §III A cont., content/cause distinction): Caston unpacks (3). 'Like by like' addresses two questions usually run together: (i) how is a certain mental state BROUGHT ABOUT (the causal question); (ii) what is the resulting state about, i.e., what is its CONTENT? On Empedocles' view, fiery effluences flow from a fire and meet the like material in the eye — both content and cause are explained: cause = the actual fire, content = the actually-present 'fire' in the eye. Content is determined by what brings the mental state about — like-affected-by-like. Caston separates the two sub-theses: (3a) one perceives or thinks whenever like is affected by like; (3b) whatever one perceives or thinks on a given occasion corresponds exactly to whatever brings that state about. (3a) and (3b) are LOGICALLY INDEPENDENT. Anaxagoras accepts (3b) without (3a). From (3b) alone: (4) whatever one perceives or thinks on a given occasion corresponds exactly to something in the environment. If (3b) applies to all mental states, error is IMPOSSIBLE.

Cluster 12 (PDF 10, book 30, §III A cont.): The restriction strategy. To allow for error, an adherent of (3) must RESTRICT it to veridical mental states (apply the type but not every token). On this reading, (5) reduces to the tautology that all veridical appearances are veridical. The price is a LACUNA in the story of content for nonveridical states. Since these still occur as the result of SOME interaction, they must be due to interaction of UNLIKES — just as Aristotle says in the second horn. The dilemma is genuine, brought about by (3) understood as a thesis about mental states IN GENERAL.

Cluster 13 (PDF 10-11, book 30-31, §III B 'Second Horn'): Aristotle cannot rule the second horn out as absurd. He acknowledges error. The compressed objection: 'both error and knowledge of contraries seem to be the same' (427b5-6). This is not Aristotle's own view but what he takes to follow from the second horn. Reconstruction: if error were the interaction of unlikes, then in cases of contraries (one knows pairs of contraries because contrary state is recognized from its contrary, EN 5.1, 1129a17ff., DA 3.6, 430b21-24, DA 1.5, 411a3-7), error and knowledge would coincide — absurd. So error cannot be due to interaction of unlikes. The reductio relies on a tacit premise (the contraries-rule); Aristotle's opponents are free to deny it but won't be troubled — Aristotle takes such ad-hominem refusal as eristical.

Cluster 14 (PDF 11, book 31, §III B closing): The dilemma's further significance: Aristotle, if faced with it himself, COULD NOT ACCEPT THE SECOND HORN. He is therefore driven toward the FIRST HORN — something he considers anathema. The problem of error constitutes the real challenge for him.

Cluster 15 (PDF 11-12, book 32-34, §IV): The thesis that all appearances are true does NOT follow from (1) alone but from premises Aristotle supplies to support it. Caston identifies (6) thinking and perceiving are both alterations (ἀλλοιώσεις). Metaph. 4.5, 1009b12-17: 'because they suppose perception is thought and this is alteration, perceptual appearance is of necessity true' — the route Aristotle takes there is wider than DA 3.3's. (6) captures Anaxagoras (incorporeal intellect) and Theophrastus' summary of Empedocles/Democritus.

Cluster 16 (PDF 12-13, book 34-36, §IV cont., Anaxagoras): The exception. Anaxagoras is not a materialist (DA 1.2, 405a16-17; 3.4, 429a18); his intellect is 'simple, unmixed, and pure'; he 'has nothing in common with anything' (DA 1.2, 405b21; 3.4, 429b24). Anaxagoras cannot endorse (3a) but can accept (3b) — content determined by what brings the state about (Aristotle's interpretation in DA 1.2, 405a16-17 + 3.4, 429a18). Aristotle's problem with predecessors thus has nothing to do with whether cognition is a bodily process or not, nor depends on details of like-by-like theories. All that is required is that a theory make thinking and perceiving 'alterations.'

Cluster 17 (PDF 13, book 36, §IV cont., Theophrastus, Parmenides, Democritus): Theophrastus on Parmenides (De sens. 3, 499.14-16 Diels Doxogr.): 'whenever the hot or cold preponderates, thought comes to be different' — body-state determines content. Homer (Od. 18.136 contextualized by Theophrastus): thought changes with bodily condition. Democritus (Theophrastus De sens. 60-67, 73-78, 515.13-519.4, 520.24-522.25 Diels Doxogr.): the perceptual experiences resulting from atomic features are not the way things actually are. Aristotle reads Democritus as vacillating between 'every appearance true' and 'no appearance is' (Metaph. 4.5, 1009b11-12; 1.2, 404a27-31; cf. Theophrastus De sens. 69, 519.19-22 Diels Doxogr., fn. 40).

Cluster 18 (PDF 13-14, book 37-38, §IV closing): Aristotle's deepest diagnosis: the problem is that predecessors offer no account of the CONTENT of mental states that goes beyond this simple causal interaction. If content always corresponds to cause, error is impossible; if content has no relation to cause at all, error is again unaccountable (the worry behind nominalism/antirealism). Error requires that content bear SOME relation to cause, but content and cause MUST BE ABLE TO DIVERGE. The relation between a mental state and what it is about cannot be simply identified with the relation between an effect and its cause. The dilemma's logic: predecessors are stuck with cause=content; Aristotle must show how to differentiate.

Cluster 19 (PDF 14, book 38, §V opening): Aristotle's commitment to (1). DA 3.4, 429a16-17: 'the intellect is related to the objects of conception in just the same way as the sense can sense to the objects of sense.' This is just what leads to the dilemma — and the various disanalogies (intellect not the activity of a bodily organ, DA 3.4 429a18-27; De gen. anim. 2.3, 736b28-29, against (2)) do not free him. As shown, incorporeality does not explain how error is possible.

Cluster 20 (PDF 14, book 39, §V cont.): Aristotle's commitment to (3). At DA 2.5, theorists like Anaxagoras are right only insofar as the sense must INITIALLY be unlike the object in actuality (to interact), but the sense must also be POTENTIALLY like and during sensation BECOMES like (417a17-20, 418a3-6; 3.2, 425b22-23). So Aristotle only rules out versions of (3a) demanding actual likeness at the BEGINNING. The likeness occurring during sensation shows he is fully committed to the cause-content correspondence: sensation is clearly about its cause. DA 3.4 frames conceiving similarly (429a13-18); the conceptual capacity is like its objects only in potentiality; during conception it becomes like its object in actuality (430a3-5; 3.8, 431b28-29; Metaph. 12.7, 1072a30). In both sensation and conception, CONTENT AND CAUSE COINCIDE. Aristotle accepts a version of (3a). So long as these states are about what brings them about, their 'appearances' will always be true.

Cluster 21 (PDF 14-15, book 39-41, §V cont., the parallel for (6)): The same result follows for Aristotle's commitment to (6). His hesitation about describing sensation/conception as 'alterations' is entirely due to his technical usage (alteration = change away from a thing's nature). In the broader sense at issue in (6) (in a different state, ἀλλοῖος), he remains vulnerable. Sensation is a 'progression towards itself and towards realization' (εἰς αὐτὸ γὰρ ἡ ἐπίδοσις καὶ εἰς ἐντελέχειαν, DA 2.5, 417b6-7) — but this 'progress towards realization' does not affect the question of error at all. So long as the content of this realization always corresponds to its cause, his account leaves no room for error. Aristotle does not shrink from these consequences either: he concedes the first horn of the dilemma WITH REGARD TO THE MOST BASIC FORMS of perception and thought, namely SENSATION AND CONCEPTION (the sensation of proper perceptibles: DA 3.3, 427b12; 2.6, 418a11; De sens. 4, 442b8-10; Metaph. 4.5, 1010b2-3, cf. DA 3.3, 428a11; 3.4, 430b29; and the conception of incomposites/indivisibles, DA 3.6, 430a26-27, b27-28; Metaph. 9.10, 1051b15-32; 1052a1-4).

Cluster 22 (PDF 15, book 41, §V cont., the metaphor of 'making contact'): To use Aristotle's metaphor: sensation and conception are like θιγγάνειν — 'making contact' (Metaph. 9.10, 1051b24-25). They either work or not at all. In the case of sensation, Aristotle explicitly endorses a version of (3b): the object of a given act of sensation must exist (DA 2.5, 417b24-26). THERE IS A SENSE IN WHICH ALL APPEARANCES ARE TRUE FOR ARISTOTLE: namely, all those appearances that arise from sensation and conception, the most basic operations. This is the key restriction. If Aristotle thought all cognitive functioning could be explained in terms of these two states — if he accepted (3b) as a completely general thesis as his predecessors did — he would be committed to the first horn in its full scope. But (3b) holds only for certain types of mental states; for others, he can evade the disastrous consequences.

Cluster 23 (PDF 15, book 41, §V cont., the inventory of phantasia-requiring states): Aristotle clearly does NOT think every kind of mental state can be explained on the same model as sensation and conception. Virtually all mental states and processes operate differently. IMAGINATION (in visualization sense, DA 3.3, 427b17-20), association (De mem. et remin. 2, 451b10-452b7, 453a4-31), memory (DA 1.4, 408b16-17; De mem. et remin. 1, 450a10-13, 451a14-17; Rhet. 1, 1370a29-30), expectation (Rhet. 1.11, 1370a29-30; 2.5, 1383a17-19), thought (DA 1, 403a8-10), reasoning (DA 3.10, 433b10-12, b27-29), deliberation (DA 3.7, 431b6-8; 3.11, 434a7-10), desire (DA 3.10, 433b10-12, b27-29; De motu an. 8, 702a18f.), action (De motu an. 8, 702a18; 10, 703b18ff.), passions (Rhet. 2.5, 1382a21-22, 1383a18-19; 2.6, 1384a22; cf. De motu an. 8, 702a18; 10, 703b18f.), dreams (De insomn. 1, 459a18-21; 3, 462a16, a29-31) — ALL require phantasia (fn. 46 p. 41). Imagination, association, memory, expectation, thought, reasoning, deliberation, desire, action, passions, dreams. The whole catalogue of cognitive life beyond bare sensation/conception. And, Aristotle argues in the bulk of DA 3.3, phantasia cannot be identified with sensation or conception. Phantasia and all those mental states, in contrast, can be at variance with reality.

Cluster 24 (PDF 15-16, book 42-43, §V closing, conclusion of the diagnostic): Nor does the simple causal model apply to most of what we would call THOUGHT either. Anything that involves predication, negation, inference, goes beyond the most basic operation of the intellect — the conception of simple uncombined concepts. Only the latter is infallible; the rest admits of truth and falsehood (fn. 45). Even on the ordinary recognition of objects, the flower cannot AS A FLOWER be perceived by sense alone, but only INCIDENTALLY (κατὰ συμβεβηκός, 418a9); 'this form of perception requires the cooperation of other cognitive functions: memory and association at the very least, and in the case of humans, also concepts, language, and inference on occasion' (fn. 48, citing Cashdollar 1973 contra Modrak and Wedin). Aristotle thus has the means for evading the dilemma. By construing 'perceiving' and 'thinking' more narrowly than his predecessors, he leaves room for error; and by invoking a new mental state whose content can be false as well as true, used in other mental states, he provides a basis for explaining error AND content quite generally. All this assumes phantasia is not, like Molière's virtus dormativa (fn. — alluding to the satirical 'dormitive virtue' diagnosis), just a problem redescribed as a solution.

Cluster 25 (PDF 16, book 43-44, §VI): Aristotle's strategy. (1) phantasia not identical with sensation/conception; (2) its content explained differently. In 427b6-428b9 he runs a battery distinguishing phantasia from sensation (a, 428a5-18), conception (b, 428a17), knowledge (c, 428a18), belief (d, 427b16-24, 428a18-24), and a complex of belief and sensation (e, 428a24-b9, Plato Soph. 264AB / Tim. 52A). Outside the chapter, in DA 3.9, Aristotle makes the universal claim that phantasia 'differs in being from all the other [parts of soul]' (ᾧ τῷ μὲν εἶναι πάντων ἕτερον, 432a31-b1) whether or not always coinstantiated with the others. The distinction matters because phantasia is always coinstantiated with the capacity for sensation though they differ in being (τῷ εἶναι, De insomn. 1, 459a16-18).

Cluster 26 (PDF 16, book 44, §VI cont., the two argument types): Two kinds of nonidentity argument: (i) extensional — show the two powers are not always coinstantiated (not all animals think: 427b7-8, b12-14); phantasia exists where reason does not (λόγος, 428a24, b13-14) — so phantasia ≠ belief. Phantasia vs. sensation extension is less clear: 'there seem to be' animals with sensation but not phantasia (δοκεῖ, 428b8-11), though evidence outside the chapter commits Aristotle to strict coextension (fn. 9 p. 23, citing 2.2, 413b22-23; 2.3, 414b14-15; 3.11, 434a30-b4 with DA 3.3, 428a10-11). (ii) the more powerful nonidentity argument considers DIFFERENCES IN NATURE independently of questions of extension. The most decisive characteristic: FALSEHOOD. Sensation, conception, knowledge are always true (427b12, 428a11-12, a17-18). Phantasia can be false (428a11-12, b17-18). Belief can be false too (428a12, b17). Hence phantasia must be distinct from all three. The only candidate also capable of falsehood is belief.

Cluster 27 (PDF 16-17, book 44-45, §VI cont., phantasia vs. belief): But phantasia and belief differ significantly. (i) Phantasia has wider extension (every animal that has belief also has phantasia, but not vice versa); belief is a kind of accepting (ὑπόληψις, 427b24-26); there is no acceptance without conviction (427b15-16); some animals have phantasia but lack belief (so lack conviction). (ii) Aristotle takes every action to be the effect of a cognitive/desiderative pair, but he does not take these to be belief and desire — that would overintellectualize animal psychology. (iii) Belief is constrained: one cannot believe just anything but only what one judges to be right (428a23-24, 427b20-21); phantasia, in contrast, allows imaging-up freely independently of one's views about what is true (427b17-20). Sometimes belief and phantasia are independent: even knowing the sun to be larger than the inhabited world, it still appears a foot long. Phantasia is neither pure belief nor a combination of belief and sensation. Belief requires our taking the content as true (in the stronger sense of being misled, fn. 5); phantasia does not — phantasia is something different from assertion and denial (3.8, 432a10-11). Because phantasia can function apart from acceptance, it can remain emotionally unaffected by its contents (3.3, 427a23-24); belief, in contrast, affects us immediately (427a21-22). Phantasia is more basic than the intellectual powers, extends throughout the animal kingdom, capable of error, doesn't require conviction, bears content in a neutral way.

Cluster 28 (PDF 17-18, book 46-47, §VII Phantasia and Error opening + aetiology): The positive aetiology. Causal factors continue to explain content, BUT differences in aetiology suggest phantasia is grounded differently than sensation, and Aristotle exploits this to account for falsehood and the consequent plasticity of animal behavior (428b10-17). The detailed aetiology and conditions of truth/falsity follow (428b20-429a8), before reaffirming key elements of the earlier account. The section ends on a conclusive note: 'regarding what phantasia is, let this suffice' (429a8-9). In sensation: an object produces an initial stimulation (αἴσθημα) in the peripheral sense organs; this change travels to the central sense organ and produces the sensory experience (αἴσθησις). But a change can give rise to FURTHER changes — indirect effects.

Cluster 29 (PDF 18, book 47-48, §VII cont., the diagrams): Diagram 1 (p. 47): the canyon echo. A shout produces (a) the initial disturbance in air → hearing; (b) a reflected disturbance off the canyon wall → hearing-of-echo. Diagram 2 (p. 48): the phantasma. Object (αἰσθητόν) → Sensory Stimulation (αἴσθημα) in peripheral organ → Experience (αἴσθησις) in central organ; also Sensory Stimulation → Phantasma → Experience. The phantasma is the indirect, reflected effect — like the echo. Phantasma is only an INDIRECT effect of the object of perception. The phantasma is directly caused by the αἴσθημα. But the phantasma is only a SIDE-EFFECT of the primary effect (the sensory experience in the central organ). The manner of production ensures it will be a similar sort of change — can travel to and affect the central organ in similar ways. Phantasma will have similar causal powers to the sensory stimulation. It will produce experiences phenomenally like perceptual experiences, including being about what a sensation is about (ὧν αἴσθησις, DA 3.3, 428b1-2), even if the object is not in view.

Cluster 30 (PDF 18, book 48-49, §VII cont., causal divergence): Unlike sensation, phantasia is NOT about its cause (the αἴσθημα, the stimulation of peripheral organs) — ordinarily about the EXTERNAL OBJECT that causes that stimulation, the cause of its cause. But this will not happen in every case. A CAUSAL CHAIN TRACING BACK TO THE OBJECT IS NOT ESSENTIAL AT ALL. What determines the content of a phantasma is not its causal antecedents but its CAUSAL POWERS — sometimes 'modified' on its way to the central organ in a way that ALTERS these causal powers. Aristotle mentions this in explaining alcohol and sickness effects (De insomn. 3, 461a8-24; Probl. 30.14, 957a5-15, a25-35).

Cluster 31 (PDF 18, book 49, §VII cont., salamander/dragon): The vivid example. Observations of a salamander earlier in the day might produce echoes (phantasmata) remaining in the system unnoticed for hours. When reactivated in the evening, the effects of a half-bottle of whiskey may have altered them so the dreamer dreams not of a salamander but of an immense fire-breathing dragon. A dragon could not have been a causal ancestor (dragons don't exist). But the phantasmata have the ability to affect the central organ the way it WOULD be affected were the dreamer to see such a dragon. The causal history is thus NOT RELEVANT, except per accidens — at most, it could explain why phantasmata have the causal powers they happen to have. Their content is rather a function of the causal powers they actually do have at a given moment, however they came by them.

Cluster 32 (PDF 18, book 50, §VII cont., formal account P): Caston's formalization. (P): For any phantasma φ and time t, the total effect φ can produce at t on the central sense organ is the same as the total effect some sensory stimulation s could produce at t on the central sense organ, were s to occur; and at t, φ is about whatever s would be about. The sensory stimulation s will normally be the original stimulation from which φ causally derives, in which case φ is about the object that initially causes s. But this need not be the case. φ's causal powers may no longer be like those of the original stimulation, or like those of ANY actual stimulation past, present, or future, but only some merely possible one. φ will then be about whatever s would be about, were s to occur; this might be different from the way things actually are. The content of phantasia can DIVERGE COMPLETELY from its causal ancestry and from what is actually the case more widely. Phantasia can be false.

Cluster 33 (PDF 18, book 50-51, §VII cont., textual confirmation): De insomn. 2, 460b18-27: 'something falsely appears not only when an object of perception is effecting change, but also when the sense is undergoing change itself — whenever, that is, it should happen to be changed in just the same way as [it would be] by an object of perception' (460b23-25, cf. 459a1-5). Metaph. 5.29, 1024b23-24: a scene-painting and a dream are both 'something, but not what they produce a phantasia of' (τι ἀλλ' οὐχ ὧν ἐμποιεῖ τὴν φαντασίαν). Scene-paintings and dreams produce mental states not about themselves but about something quite different, splitting content and cause. Resulting states will often be false; their causes can be called false by synecdoche.

Cluster 34 (PDF 18, book 51, §VII closing, intentionality and quasi-perceptual): Three consequences. (i) Aristotle ties content of phantasia to content of sensation. Initially the content of phantasia is exactly similar to the content of the sensation that spawned it. But later changes are relevant only in comparison with the causal powers of possible sensations. This close linkage ensures the content of phantasia remains QUASI-PERCEPTUAL — similar in TYPE of information. Phantasmata can correctly be described as 'imagistic' or 'pictorial': capable of producing experiences phenomenally like perceptual experiences. (ii) Critical: phantasmata are NOT THEMSELVES VIEWED, nor are they tiny pictures of objects in the world. They are CHANGES in the perceptual system, in virtue of their causal powers. (iii) The phenomenal experience need NOT actually occur for the phantasma to have the content it does — phantasma is constituted by causal powers, not by manifest experience.

Cluster 35 (PDF 18-19, book 52, §VII closing cont., the type of falsehood): The type of falsehood at issue in phantasia is SIGNIFICANTLY DIFFERENT from the falsehood Aristotle finds in language and discursive thought. Linguistic falsehood is due to a COMBINATION of concepts that differs from how things are combined in the world (Metaph. 9.10, 1051b1-6; cf. Metaph. 6.4, 1027b20-22; DA 3.6, 430b1-2). But combination is not at issue here. Nor are concepts (DA 3.8, 432a10-14). This is significant since it allows for an account of intentionality that does NOT presuppose the conceptual structure that makes language and thought possible. It can account for intentional states that fall below this threshold (DA 3.3, 428b16-17, 429a5-6 — humans 3.7-3.8). Deliberation and higher cognition require concepts and inference, but even here Aristotle insists the functions build upon phantasia. The content of even the simplest thought is not identical with the content of any phantasma (3.8, 432a12-14); but the former depends on the latter. The forms which are thought are 'in' phantasmata (3.7, 431b2; 3.8, 432a4-6, a12-14; 431a14-16). By making phantasia the common currency among mental states rather than belief, Aristotle emphasizes a form of intentionality more BASIC than the conceptual, firmly rooted in the general character of perceptual experience.

Cluster 36 (PDF 16, book 52-53, §VIII Phantasia and Reliability): Conditions of reliability (428b17-30). The truth of phantasia depends on type of perception involved (428b17-27): proper perceptibles (colors, flavors), common perceptibles (shapes, motion), or incidental perceptibles. The latter two are already error-prone due to involvement of other fallible mental states including phantasia. For proper perceptibles, Aristotle repeats the position that sensation of them is always true (DA 3.3, 427b12, 428a11; 2.6, 418a11; De sens. 4, 442b8-10; Metaph. 4.5, 1010b2-3) but with the qualification 'or it has falsehood to the least possible extent' (ἢ ὅτι ὀλίγιστον ἔχουσα τὸ ψεῦδος, 428b19). This qualification is inexplicable on Aristotle's account UNLESS phantasia is implicated; the staring-at-white-or-green example (De insomn. 1, 459b7-13) makes the involvement of phantasia clear. The error can be explained without requiring change in the core account of sensation.

Cluster 37 (PDF 16, book 53, §VIII cont., reliability correlations): Phantasia generated by sensation will differ in reliability depending on which sort of perception is involved. Most reliable: phantasia both generated from and concurrent with sensation of proper perceptibles (428b27-28). Being concurrent with perception is no longer a guarantee of truth when phantasia is generated from the other forms of perception (428b28-29). Worst case: objects very distant (428b29-30) — perception of size and magnitude most error-prone (428b24-25). Caston flags Aristotle's surprising consequences (fn. 69): a phantasia originating from a false sensation of a proper object will be true so long as concurrent; a phantasia originating from a true perception of a common/incidental object will be false even if concurrent. Difficult to see the rationale. The remarks depend on contingent assumptions about how perception/phantasia typically function in real-world situations — not part of the account of HOW phantasia is capable of error in the first place.

Cluster 38 (PDF 17, book 54, §IX Conclusion): The beginning of DA 3.3 tells us — not too surprisingly — what the chapter is about. Aristotle's predecessors are unable to account for error because they rely on an overly simplistic account of content, one binding content too closely to cause. Aristotle's own account of sensation and conception is prey to the SAME problem. Though he does not advertise candidly, he sets about doing what needs to be done. Some mental capacities being infallible is acceptable — even foundational ones — so long as the content of OTHER mental states is not accounted for in the same way. Aristotle introduces a new capacity, NOT identical with sensation or conception; though it depends on sensation (causally and in content), the resulting analysis successfully evades the dilemma. The MORE COMPLICATED AETIOLOGY (causal POWERS rather than causal ancestors) provides an account that does not require the existence of the object — framed subjunctively, in terms of the type of effects an object WOULD have on the central sensory organ IF it were sensed. Sufficient for basic kinds of error, providing a basis for content of most intentional states WITHOUT appealing to concepts or predication.

Cluster 39 (PDF 18, book 54-55, §IX Conclusion final paragraph): The polemical close. Phantasia is NOT, then, a locus of 'non-paradigmatic sensory experience' (Schofield 1978's phrase at fn. 70). Aristotle's point is precisely that error is SO COMMONPLACE, so NORMAL, in animal life, that psychology must account for it. This cannot be done on the causal account Aristotle offers for sensation and conception. To account for ordinary, paradigmatic animal behavior, a higher degree of intentionality is required — one which makes error possible — and this requires phantasia. The crucial question remains whether this account forms the basis for a fully adequate theory of content. That question awaits another occasion (forward references to Caston 'Aristotle and the Problem of Intentionality' and The Problem of Intentionality in Ancient Greek Philosophy, Cambridge UP, fn. 67). Closing acknowledgments and 'Brown University.'

concepts.gloss: Caston's master thesis: Aristotle introduces phantasia in DA 3.3 to solve the problem of error — to preempt charges that his own theory of sensation/conception cannot explain how mental content can diverge from world

concepts.label: problem of error
concepts.gloss: The problem of explaining how the content of mental states can ever diverge from what is actually in the world — Caston's identification of DA 3.3's central concern

concepts.label: (1) thinking-as-perceiving thesis
concepts.gloss: The endoxon Aristotle attacks: thinking consists in the same KIND of process as perceiving

concepts.label: (1') strict identity thesis
concepts.gloss: Stronger version of (1): thinking does not differ from perceiving in any way at all

concepts.label: (2) bodily-process thesis
concepts.gloss: First support for (1): thinking and perceiving are both bodily processes

concepts.label: (3) like-by-like thesis
concepts.gloss: Second support for (1) and the load-bearing thesis: one thinks and perceives like by like

concepts.label: (3a) like-affected-by-like sub-thesis
concepts.gloss: First decomposition of (3): one perceives or thinks whenever like is AFFECTED by like — the causal half

concepts.label: (3b) cause-content correspondence sub-thesis
concepts.gloss: Second decomposition of (3): whatever one perceives or thinks on a given occasion corresponds EXACTLY to whatever brings that state about — the content half; logically independent of (3a)

concepts.label: (5) every-appearance-true thesis (Protagorean antirealism)
concepts.gloss: First horn of dilemma: all appearances are true — what (3) implies if applied generally; the target of the Theaetetus and Metaph. 4.5 critiques

concepts.label: (6) thinking-and-perceiving-as-alterations thesis
concepts.gloss: Wider premise from Metaph. 4.5: thinking and perceiving are both ἀλλοιώσεις — used by Aristotle to capture Anaxagoras even though he denies (2) and (3a)

concepts.label: (P) formal causal-powers account of phantasma content
concepts.gloss: Caston's formalization: for any phantasma φ and time t, the total effect φ can produce at t on the central sense organ = the total effect some sensory stimulation s could produce, were s to occur; and at t, φ is about whatever s would be about

concepts.label: the dilemma (DA 3.3 427b2-5)
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's reductio dilemma: predecessors must accept either (i) all appearances true or (ii) error = contact with what is unlike; both unacceptable

concepts.label: Aristotle's self-implication
concepts.gloss: Caston's signature move: the critique of predecessors REBOUNDS on Aristotle himself, who is committed to versions of (1), (3a), (3b), and (6) for sensation and conception

concepts.label: the restriction strategy
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's evasion: concede first horn ONLY for the most basic operations (sensation of proper perceptibles, conception of incomposites), and explain content of OTHER mental states via phantasia, with a different aetiology

concepts.label: causal antecedents vs. causal powers
concepts.gloss: The core innovation: a phantasma's content is determined not by what actually caused it (causal ancestry) but by what type of sensory stimulation it has the causal powers to mimic; permits content-cause divergence

concepts.label: phantasia as 'echo' of sensation
concepts.gloss: Caston's analogy via Diagram 1 (p. 47): like a canyon echo, phantasma is an indirect, reflected effect of the original stimulation in the air, capable of producing hearing again

concepts.label: salamander-to-dragon counterexample
concepts.gloss: Caston's illustrative example showing causal-history irrelevance: a phantasma originating in salamander-observation, modified by whiskey, can come to be about a fire-breathing dragon — an object that need never have been perceived nor exist

concepts.label: quasi-perceptual character of phantasia
concepts.gloss: Phantasmata are similar in TYPE of information to sensation: imagistic/pictorial in capacity, but NOT themselves viewed, NOT tiny pictures — they are CHANGES in the perceptual system, individuated by causal powers

concepts.label: non-propositional intentionality
concepts.gloss: Phantasia's content is not propositional, not the combination-falsehood of language/discursive thought (Metaph. 9.10), but a non-conceptual misalignment of cause and content — a more basic form of intentionality

concepts.label: phantasia as common currency
concepts.gloss: Caston's framing: by making phantasia (rather than belief) the common substrate of mental states, Aristotle emphasizes a form of intentionality MORE BASIC than the conceptual, rooted in the general character of perceptual experience

concepts.label: the infallibility of basic operations
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's concession of first horn for sensation of proper perceptibles and conception of incomposites/indivisibles — explicitly bitten as a bullet

concepts.label: θιγγάνειν / making-contact metaphor
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's metaphor (Metaph. 9.10, 1051b24-25) for the all-or-nothing character of basic sensation and conception: they either work or not at all — supporting the infallibility of these basic operations

concepts.label: phantasia distinct in being (τῷ εἶναι)
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's mode of non-identity (DA 3.9, 432a31-b1; De insomn. 1, 459a16-18): two powers always coinstantiated may still differ in being; Caston identifies as a category of nonidentity argument

concepts.label: πίστις (conviction) as differentia of belief
concepts.gloss: Belief requires conviction (πίστις); phantasia does not; conviction does not occur without reason (λόγος); so non-rational animals have phantasia but not belief

concepts.label: Caston's contra-Schofield: phantasia is not non-paradigmatic
concepts.gloss: Polemical close: Schofield 1978's framing of phantasia as locus of 'non-paradigmatic sensory experience' is rejected — error is so normal in animal life that psychology must account for it

concepts.label: phantasia as basis for higher cognition
concepts.gloss: Even deliberation and conceptual thought build on phantasia — the content of thought is 'in' phantasmata (DA 3.7-3.8); phantasia provides the substrate for predication/inference

concepts.label: the Anaxagoras case
concepts.gloss: Anaxagoras is the limit case: intellect is incorporeal so rejects (2), and intellect 'has nothing in common with anything' so rejects (3a); but accepts (3b) — content determined by cause — and so is still committed to (5)

concepts.label: Aristotle's interpretive charity to predecessors
concepts.gloss: Caston's reading: Aristotle imputes commitment to (3) and (5) to predecessors even when not explicit; reads them as 'committed to' rather than 'asserting'

concepts.label: two nonidentity argument-types in DA 3.3
concepts.gloss: (i) Extensional: powers not always coinstantiated; (ii) differing in being: powers always coinstantiated but distinct in essence — Caston's analytic taxonomy

concepts.label: infallibility-of-proper-perceptibles + ὀλίγιστον qualification
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's qualification at 428b19 — sensation of proper perceptibles is always true OR has falsehood to the least possible extent — only explicable on Caston's account if phantasia is implicated

concepts.label: phantasia's universal applicability inventory
concepts.gloss: Caston's catalogue (fn. 46 p. 41): imagination, association, memory, expectation, thought, reasoning, deliberation, desire, action, passions, dreams — all require phantasia

concepts.label: the dual derivation thesis
concepts.gloss: Phantasia derives from sensation in two respects: (i) CAUSALLY derives from a particular sensation; (ii) its CHARACTER derives from the character of that sensation

readings.label: Functional-explanatory reading: phantasia solves the problem of error
readings.thesis: Aristotle introduces phantasia in DA 3.3 NOT to introduce a special faculty of mental imagery or 'imagination' in the empiricist sense, but to solve a structural explanatory problem: his own theory of sensation/conception inherits the same cause-content correspondence that doomed his predecessors to either (5) all-appearances-true or (ii) error-as-unlike-by-unlike. Phantasia, with its more complex aetiology (causal powers, not causal ancestors), allows Aristotle to concede the first horn for the most basic operations while explaining error and the content of higher intentional states through a distinct capacity.
readings.diverges_from: Schofield 1978's reading of phantasia as locus of 'non-paradigmatic sensory experience' (explicitly contested, fn. 70); Modrak's Phantasia Reconsidered and Aristotle: The Power of Perception (Modrak claims Aristotle DOES offer an account of sensation that explains the failure of intersubstitutivity — contested fn. 7); Wedin's Mind and Imagination on phantasia as condition of sensation of proper perceptibles (contested fn. 49)

readings.label: Causal-powers (not causal-ancestors) reading of phantasma content
readings.thesis: The content of a phantasma is determined by its CAUSAL POWERS — its capacity to affect the central sense organ in ways indistinguishable from particular sensory stimulations — NOT by its actual causal antecedents. This is the key innovation distinguishing phantasia from sensation/conception, which retain the cause-content correspondence. Subjunctive formulation: φ is about WHATEVER s WOULD be about, were s to occur — even if s never occurs, and even if no object answering s ever existed.
key_anchors: Metaph. 5.29, 1024b23-24 (scene-painting/dream are 'something but not what they produce a phantasia of')
Diagram 2 (p. 48): phantasma as side-effect of αἴσθημα
readings.diverges_from: Pictorial/imagistic readings that treat phantasmata as mental pictures (Modrak; arguably Wedin); causal-history accounts of mental content that require an actual chain back to the represented object

readings.label: Phantasia as non-propositional intentionality
readings.thesis: The type of falsehood at issue in phantasia is significantly different from propositional/linguistic falsehood (Metaph. 9.10, 1051b1-6 — combination-falsehood). Phantasia's content is non-propositional: it does NOT presuppose concepts, predication, or the combination/separation that makes language and thought possible. It can account for intentional states below this conceptual threshold (animal mental life, much of human prereflective life). By making phantasia (not belief) the common currency among mental states, Aristotle emphasizes a form of intentionality more basic than the conceptual, rooted in the general character of perceptual experience.
key_anchors: DA 3.3, 429a5-6 (men act on phantasia when mind clouded)
readings.diverges_from: Frede 1992's 'Cognitive Role of Phantasia' (Caston engages but diverges on degree of intellectualist content); Modrak's propositional reading of phantasia (Phantasia Reconsidered — Caston cites fn. 55 as a target)

readings.label: Aristotle's self-implication and the restriction strategy
readings.thesis: Aristotle's critique of his predecessors REBOUNDS on him. He is committed to versions of (1) thinking-like-perceiving, (3a) like-affected-by-like, (3b) cause-content correspondence, and (6) thinking-and-perceiving-as-alterations — at least for sensation and conception. He cannot accept the second horn (error-as-unlike-by-unlike) and is driven toward the first (all appearances true). His evasion: concede first horn ONLY for the most basic operations (sensation of proper perceptibles; conception of incomposites/indivisibles) and account for content of OTHER mental states via phantasia, whose aetiology permits content-cause divergence. The infallibility of basic operations is a feature, not a bug — explicitly bitten as a bullet via the θιγγάνειν metaphor (Metaph. 9.10, 1051b24-25).
readings.diverges_from: Readings that treat Aristotle's predecessor-critique as comfortably external (not self-implicating); readings that deny Aristotle's infallibilism about proper perceptibles

readings.label: Phantasia as foundational for higher cognition
readings.thesis: Phantasia is not merely a side-faculty for dreams and illusions; it is the substrate of higher cognition. Memory, expectation, reasoning, deliberation, desire, action, passions — all require phantasia. Even deliberation and conceptual thought build on phantasia: the forms which are thought are 'in' phantasmata (DA 3.7, 431b2; 3.8, 432a4-6, a12-14; 431a14-16). Phantasia thus provides the BASIC INTENTIONAL CURRENCY of the soul.
key_anchors: De motu an. 7, 701b17-22 (phantasia and thought have power of objects)
readings.diverges_from: Narrowly intellectualist readings of Aristotle's psychology that downplay phantasia's foundational role (potentially Wedin); empiricist-readings that treat phantasia as merely passive image-storage

tensions.label: Aristotle's infallibilism vs. the omnipresence of error
tensions.description: Aristotle holds sensation of proper perceptibles is always true (DA 3.3, 427b12; 2.6, 418a11; De sens. 4, 442b8-10; Metaph. 4.5, 1010b2-3) AND that animals spend MORE time in error than in veridical cognition (DA 3.3, 427a29-b2, with comparative force οἰκειότερον/πλείω, fn. 20). The infallibility of basic operations is preserved at the cost of relocating all the heavy lifting of intentionality to phantasia.

tensions.label: Causal antecedents vs. causal powers
tensions.description: Phantasia must allow content-cause divergence (else falsehood is impossible), but must also be 'about' something rather than nothing (else intentionality fails). Caston's resolution: content is determined by what kind of sensation φ's causal powers WOULD MIMIC, even if no such sensation occurs. This subjunctive/possibility-based account departs from the causal-history models standard in late-20th-century philosophy of mind.

tensions.label: The reliability paradoxes of DA 3.3, 428b27-30
tensions.description: Aristotle's correlations among types-of-perception, concurrence, and reliability yield bizarre consequences (fn. 69): (i) phantasia originating from a FALSE sensation of a proper object is TRUE so long as concurrent; (ii) phantasia originating from a TRUE perception of a common/incidental object is FALSE even if concurrent. Caston flags but does not fully resolve.

tensions.label: Two non-identity criteria — extensional vs. in-being
tensions.description: Aristotle deploys both arguments-from-non-coinstantiation (extensional) and arguments-from-difference-in-being (τῷ εἶναι). The latter (DA 3.9, 432a31-b1; De insomn. 1, 459a16-18) shows phantasia and αἰσθητικόν can be the SAME power yet distinct — a paraphrase-resistant non-Leibnizian identity criterion (fn. 51 on Leibniz's Law). Caston notes the criterion functions like a distinction of essence/aspect.

tensions.label: Belief's normative constraint vs. phantasia's freedom
tensions.description: Belief is bound to what one judges to be the case (428a23-24, 427b20-21); phantasia is free to image-up independently of belief (427b17-20). Yet phantasia underlies higher cognition, including belief. The puzzle: how can the free, image-permissive faculty be the substrate of the constrained, conviction-bound one? Aristotle's answer: phantasia is the COMMON CURRENCY whose content can later be ACCEPTED (belief) or REMAIN UNACCEPTED (mere imaging) — but the divergence-potential is itself the explanatory advantage.

interlocutors.label: Empedocles
interlocutors.role: the canonical Presocratic theorist of like-by-like via fiery effluences (DK 31 B 106, B 108, A 86); Aristotle's chief stalking horse for the (3a)+(3b) commitments

interlocutors.label: Parmenides
interlocutors.role: cited via Theophrastus (De sens. 3) on body-balance determining thought; canonical exception (Met. 4.5, 1009b17-31) along with Empedocles, Anaxagoras, Democritus

interlocutors.label: Anaxagoras
interlocutors.role: the limit case of (3b) without (3a); intellect 'simple, unmixed, and pure' (DA 1.2, 405a16-17); rejects bodily-process (2), rejects like-affected-by-like (3a), but accepts cause-content correspondence (3b)

interlocutors.label: Democritus
interlocutors.role: atomist who held perceptual qualities are not in the way things are in actual fact (Theophrastus De sens. 60-67, 73-78); Aristotle reads as vacillating between every-appearance-true and no-appearance-true (Metaph. 4.5, 1009b11-12; fn. 40)

interlocutors.label: Homer
interlocutors.role: cited at DA 3.3, 427a24-26 (Odyssey 18.136) and via Theophrastus on the Hector-fragment (Iliad 23) for bodily-condition determining thought

interlocutors.label: Protagoras
interlocutors.role: the master target of the every-appearance-true antirealism; the unnamed shadow throughout DA 3.3 and explicitly the Theaetetus context (Burnyeat 1990)

interlocutors.label: Plato (Theaetetus, Sophist, Timaeus, Phaedo)
interlocutors.role: the immediate Platonic precursor: Theaetetus on knowledge-is-perception/all-appearances-true/Secret Doctrine; Sophist 264AB on phantasia as belief-sensation complex; Timaeus 52A; Phaedo on corporeality and infallibility

interlocutors.label: Theophrastus
interlocutors.role: the doxographical channel; provides the De sensibus summaries of Empedocles, Parmenides, Anaxagoras, Democritus; gives the τὸ αὐτὸν ἢ παραπαλήσιον formula (De sens. 10) supporting Caston's weak reading of (1)

nussbaum_white_comparison.convergence_with_nussbaum_1985: Caston and Nussbaum 1985 agree (1) that phantasia is necessary for action and most non-foundational mental states (Caston's catalogue at fn. 46 — imagination, association, memory, expectation, thought, reasoning, deliberation, desire, action, passions, dreams — substantially overlaps Nussbaum's 'phantasia in action' inventory); (2) that phantasia is a 'horizontal' faculty cutting across the perception/thought divide rather than a 'vertical' level between them; (3) that the textual evidence in De Motu Animalium 6-7 + DA 3.3-3.11 must be read together. Both reject the reductive identification of phantasia with mental imagery in the empiricist sense.
nussbaum_white_comparison.divergence_from_nussbaum_1985: Caston's emphasis is sharply different: where Nussbaum reads phantasia as the faculty enabling 'seeing-as' and the practical-syllogistic mediation between desire and action, Caston reads phantasia primarily as a solution to a THEORETICAL problem in the philosophy of mind — the problem of intentional content with cause-content divergence. Nussbaum's interest is action-theoretic and ethical; Caston's is metaphysical and content-theoretical (intentionality, falsehood, antirealism). Caston cites Nussbaum's 1978 De Motu commentary in fn. 1 but does NOT engage her 1985 article (PHX-01), and his treatment of action (the brief catalogue at fn. 46 referencing De motu an. 8 and Rhet. 2.5-2.6) is markedly more cursory than his treatment of falsehood and content.
nussbaum_white_comparison.convergence_with_white_1985: Both agree (1) phantasia is grounded in sensation but distinct from it; (2) phantasia is essentially derivative — White: 'phantasia is rooted in the act of sensation' (DA 3.3, 428b10-11) / Caston: 'phantasia derives from sensation in two respects — causally and in character' (book 47); (3) phantasia subserves higher cognition (both pick up DA 3.7-3.8 on forms-in-phantasmata); (4) phantasia handles temporal mediation (White: phantasia gives stability to appearances against the now-fleetingness of aisthesis; Caston: phantasmata can persist after sensation's cause has departed, enabling memory, expectation, etc.); (5) refusal to render phantasia simply as 'imagination' in the modern sense (White is more explicit on this — Caston's title acknowledges the conventional translation but his analysis preserves Aristotle's distinctive concept).
nussbaum_white_comparison.divergence_from_white_1985: Wholly different methodologies and registers. White writes in the Thomistic-philological tradition with German philological backbone (Bonitz, Freudenthal, Hicks); Caston writes in the analytic philosophy-of-mind tradition. Where White's centerpiece is the 'picture-vs-encounter' distinction at DA 3.3, 427b21-24 (phantasia 'coolly regards' affecting scenes as one would a picture), Caston's centerpiece is the dilemma at DA 3.3, 427b2-5 and the formal causal-powers account (P). White's emphasis is on phantasia's role in NOUS (preparation for thought); Caston's is on phantasia's role in handling ERROR. White treats phantasia as ennobling — providing the 'familiar interior landscape' that orients human thinking; Caston treats it as analytically necessary — a posit required to evade an explanatory dilemma. The two essays do not cite each other (White does not cite Caston since Caston published 10 years later; Caston does not cite White, indicating no awareness or engagement). Both essays are roughly contemporaneous productions in fundamentally different scholarly cultures.
nussbaum_white_comparison.convergence_with_frede_1992: Caston cites Frede 1992 only in the opening literature footnote, but the relationship is clear: both emphasize phantasia's COGNITIVE role (Frede's title) and both resist the reduction of phantasia to mere mental imagery. Both engage Schofield, Modrak, and the Nussbaum-Rorty volume tradition.
nussbaum_white_comparison.divergence_from_frede_1992: Frede emphasizes the intellectualist dimension of phantasia — its role in concept-application and predication. Caston emphasizes the SUB-conceptual dimension — phantasia as non-propositional intentionality, the substrate of perceptual content below the threshold of language and thought. Caston's reading is more sharply anti-intellectualist about phantasia's basic operation, even while granting that higher cognition uses phantasmata.
nussbaum_white_comparison.where_caston_positions_himself: Caston positions himself as the analytic-philosophy-of-mind interpreter of Aristotle's phantasia. His targets are explicit: Schofield (phantasia-as-non-paradigmatic, rejected at fn. 70), Modrak (phantasia-as-propositional/belief-like, rejected at fns. 7 + 55 + 48), Wedin (phantasia as condition of sensation of proper perceptibles, rejected at fn. 49). His allies are Burnyeat (Theaetetus 1990, fn. 22), Cashdollar (incidental perception, fn. 48), Kenny ('Argument from Illusion', fn. 50), and Engmann (broader-falsity reading, fn. 67). The cluster picture: Caston extends Nussbaum/Frede on phantasia's cognitive role + extends Engmann on broader-falsity + contests Modrak/Wedin on intellectualist/conditional readings + contests Schofield on marginal-vs-paradigmatic status. White is invisible to Caston; the two essays are independent productions in different scholarly traditions.
